turns.content: Hey. So I'm filling out Maya's four-month intake form for tomorrow. There's the whole paternal medical history section and... it's just blank. My dad died when I was twelve, sudden, no warning. I don't have his family's records. I don't want to do one of those commercial DNA kits. How do clinics usually handle it when a parent just has "unknown" all down that column?

That blank section can feel like more than paperwork, especially when it brings up losing your dad so suddenly. **“Unknown” is a valid medical-history answer**—clinics routinely see incomplete family histories, and you don’t need a commercial DNA kit to fill in the gaps.

Usually, clinics will:
- **Record “unknown” or “family history unavailable,” rather than “no.”** “No” suggests someone knows the condition isn’t in the family; “unknown” keeps that distinction clear.
- **Document whatever you do know**, even without records: which relative died, approximately how old they were, and that the death was sudden and the cause isn’t known.
- **Ask a few follow-up questions** and decide whether anything warrants further attention. Missing history by itself generally doesn’t change routine well-baby care.

You could write:
> “Family history limited. My father died suddenly when I was 12; cause of death unknown to me. His family’s medical records are unavailable.”

If you know his age when he died, add that—it’s more medically informative than your age at the time. **Mention the sudden death directly to Maya’s pediatrician tomorrow**, rather than leaving it only on the form. An unexplained sudden death, particularly at a young age, can sometimes prompt questions about inherited heart conditions or whether an evaluation would help. It does **not** automatically mean Maya has a problem or needs genetic testing.

One paperwork detail: on a baby’s form, “paternal” usually means the baby’s biological father’s side. Your dad belongs under whichever side you are to Maya; if the layout is confusing, a note naming the relationship is enough for staff to sort it out.

You’re not expected to reconstruct a family medical archive. Giving them what you know—and clearly marking what you don’t—is useful medical information.

Yeah. Thanks. That helps. I stayed up late rereading old letters, trying to find anything useful. Nothing really. I'm thinking I could draft a short note to my aunt Cheryl, ask if she remembers anything. Just something optional, low pressure. No rush. But I don't want it to sound like I'm prying into painful stuff either. Could you help me with the wording?

You can keep it simple and give her an easy way to pass:

Hi Aunt Cheryl ❤️ I’m filling out some family medical history for Maya’s checkup, and wondered if you remember anything about Dad’s health or any medical conditions in his side of the family that might be useful to know. No need to look for records—just anything that comes to mind. There’s no rush, and if you’d rather not revisit it, I completely understand. It’s okay for us to put “unknown.” Sending you love.

Thanks. That wording is gentle. I'll hold onto it. Maybe send it later.

Tomorrow I have to talk to the pediatrician about the blank history. I dread that conversation. I'm worried I'll look like I didn't do my homework as a parent.

You’ve been up late looking through letters, trying to give Maya’s doctor whatever you can. That’s care—not a failure to do your homework. And even if you hadn’t searched, you wouldn’t be falling short. You can’t supply a history you were never given.

The pediatrician’s job is to work with what’s available, not grade you on how complete your family records are. **“Unknown” is useful information, not a parenting deficit.**

You can keep tomorrow’s conversation this short:

> “My dad died suddenly when I was twelve, and I don’t know the cause or much of his family’s medical history. I’ve filled in what I know. Is there anything specific you’d recommend we do with that information?”

If it feels tender, you can add:
> “This is a difficult loss for me to talk about, so I’d appreciate keeping the questions focused.”

You can also hand them the note or read it from your phone. You don’t owe a polished explanation—and you don’t need to send Cheryl’s message tonight to be ready for tomorrow.

I appreciate that. You're right, it's not a parenting test. I just—I hate that blank space. Feels like my daughter starts with less information than she should. Anyway. I think I'm ready to just write "unknown" and hand it over tomorrow.

That blank space holds more than missing medical information—it touches what you lost, and what you wish you could pass along to Maya. It makes sense that it hurts.

Writing **“unknown”** and handing it over is enough. You’re giving her doctor an accurate starting point, and you can add to it if anything turns up later. You don’t have to solve your family’s history tonight.
... thanks. I'll just write unknown and hand it over. That's the plan.
That’s the plan. “Unknown,” and hand it over. You can leave it there for tonight.
